read.title: Volunteering Abroad
read.text: Every year, thousands of young Israelis volunteer abroad after the army. Some teach English in rural schools; others help build houses after natural disasters. Research shows that volunteers often return with a stronger sense of purpose. However, critics argue that short trips may not always benefit local communities. Experts suggest choosing organizations that work closely with local people and that commit to long-term projects.

q.a: Short trips may not help local communities.
Choosing organizations that work with local people.

read.title: The Four-Day School Week
read.text: Some schools in the United States have adopted a four-day week in order to save money. Supporters claim that students are more rested and that teachers have time to prepare lessons. Opponents worry about working parents, who must find childcare on the fifth day. The evidence so far is mixed: in some districts grades improved, while in others there was no significant change.

q.q: Why did some schools adopt a four-day week?

read.title: Fake News
read.text: False stories spread six times faster online than true ones, according to a well-known study. One reason is emotion: shocking headlines make people angry or frightened, and they share them without checking. To protect yourself, look at the source, compare several reliable websites, and be suspicious of articles that seem designed to provoke a strong reaction.

q.q: Why do false stories spread quickly?
o: Websites pay people to share them.

q.q: Which piece of advice is given?

read.title: A Robot in the Classroom
read.text: A school in Japan recently introduced a small robot to help students practice English. The robot asks questions, corrects pronunciation and never loses patience. Teachers report that shy students are more willing to speak in front of a machine than in front of their classmates. Nevertheless, the teachers emphasize that the robot cannot replace human contact.

q.q: Why do shy students like the robot?
q.a: They are less embarrassed to speak.
A robot cannot replace human contact.

read.title: The Price of Fast Fashion
read.text: Clothing has never been cheaper, but there is a hidden cost. The fashion industry produces about ten percent of the world's carbon emissions, and many factory workers earn very low wages. Some consumers are responding by buying second-hand clothes, repairing what they own and choosing brands that are honest about their production methods.

q.q: What is the "hidden cost" of cheap clothing?

read.title: Sleep and Memory
read.text: Scientists have discovered that sleep plays an essential role in memory. While we sleep, the brain organizes the information we acquired during the day and stores it for the long term. Students who stay up all night before an exam may actually remember less. A regular sleep schedule, researchers conclude, is one of the most efficient study tools.

q.q: What does the brain do while we sleep?

read.title: City Gardens
read.text: In many urban neighborhoods, residents are turning empty lots into community gardens. Besides growing fresh vegetables, the gardens bring neighbors together and give children a chance to learn about agriculture. Elderly residents, who may feel lonely, often become the gardens' most devoted volunteers.

q.q: What do community gardens give children?
q.a: A chance to learn about agriculture.

q.q: Who are often the most devoted volunteers?

read.title: An Unusual Museum
read.text: In Zagreb, Croatia, there is a museum dedicated to broken relationships. Visitors from all over the world have donated objects that remind them of a former partner: a toaster, a wedding dress, even an axe. Each object comes with a short personal story. The museum's founders say that sharing these stories helps people cope with loss.

q.q: What is unusual about the museum?
q.a: Its objects are linked to broken relationships.

q.q: According to the founders, how does the museum help people?
q.a: It helps them cope with loss.
